title: INTERSECT & INTERSECT ALL
description: Find common rows across multiple datasets using mathematical intersection.

data.text: **`INTERSECT`** returns only the rows that appear in **both** query result sets. Just like `UNION`, `INTERSECT` removes duplicate rows by default, while `INTERSECT ALL` retains matching duplicates.

data.title: Finding Users Enrolled in Both Courses
data.content: Identifies students who completed both JavaScript and PostgreSQL courses.
data.code:
SELECT student_id 
FROM course_enrollments 
WHERE course_slug = 'javascript-fundamentals'

INTERSECT

SELECT student_id 
FROM course_enrollments 
WHERE course_slug = 'postgresql';

data.text: INTERSECT is readable, but it removes duplicates, which means the database must hash or sort both inputs. When the requirement is 'has both of these related rows' rather than 'the row values are identical', two EXISTS predicates express the intent more precisely and can use indexes on the join columns.

data.title: Same result with EXISTS
data.content: This finds students enrolled in both courses and keeps one row per student, using the index on enrollments(student_id, course).
data.code:
SELECT s.id, s.name
FROM students AS s
WHERE EXISTS (
        SELECT 1
        FROM enrollments AS e
        WHERE e.student_id = s.id
          AND e.course = 'PostgreSQL'
      )
  AND EXISTS (
        SELECT 1
        FROM enrollments AS e
        WHERE e.student_id = s.id
          AND e.course = 'JavaScript'
      )
ORDER BY s.name;

data.title: Interview angle: set semantics matter
data.text: INTERSECT works on whole rows, so it only matches when every selected column is equal. EXISTS works on a relationship, so the two rows can differ in every column except the join key. Interviewers probe this distinction with questions like 'find users who bought product A and product B'. Saying 'EXISTS twice' is the precise answer; saying 'INTERSECT' requires both queries to select the same columns.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: `INTERSECT` outputs rows that exist in both queries.
Can often be rewritten with `INNER JOIN` or `EXISTS` depending on performance requirements.
Compatible column counts and data types are required.
